paragraphs: At the hour of the hare, the bell of Xianyang Hall struck seven times. At the sixth stroke, Madam Wu of Hengtang was still tying straw sandals for her son. By the seventh, someone in the north of the city had lifted a window shutter, seen a row of lights still burning on Qin’s watchtowers, and thought the assault had finally begun.

Jiankang had been under siege for twenty-seven days. Several trading gates in the outer walls still admitted civilian boats, but the price of rice rose by the day. Weapons could not be brought into the city, and the warships coming to its aid from the river could scarcely reach shore. In some wards vegetables could still be bought by daylight; after dark soldiers came with requisition orders bearing different camp designations. The walls were quiet. Inside the city, people could hear every opening of a granary door, every pounding of a medicine mortar until there was nothing left to grind.

When Liu Yu reached the wounded men’s camp at the Eastern Headquarters, the healers had just carried a body beyond the curtain. The dead archer was seventeen. Struck by an arrow at the Fei River, he had walked back to Jiankang with his unit, only for his wound to fester a fortnight later. Madam Wu crouched beside the cot, refusing to release the hemp cord of a straw sandal. Her elder son had died years earlier fighting Huan Xuan. A clerk had copied one character of his name incorrectly into the old roll, and she had yet to receive the rice owed her.
Liu Yu stood beside her. They knew each other. She had once waited outside the military office for an entire day to see him.
“The palace is debating peace and war today,” he said.
Madam Wu bent over the sandal and tied the final knot. “Have you come to make me weep for them?”
“I’ve come so you can hear.”
“And when I’ve heard?”
“If you have something to say, someone will record it.”

She smoothed the sides of the sandal as though, once properly shod, the boy might still continue his journey. She rolled his discarded pair into the front of her robe. After a while she rose, leaned against the doorpost and said, “This time, see that his name is right on the military roll. I’ve been pleading over one surname for two years.”

The court council had been summoned for imperial kinsmen, the central offices, and the generals of the Beifu Army. But Liu Yu brought with him Ward Head Ge, Yuan Liu the Qinhuai boatman, the owner of a northern-city apothecary, two wounded soldiers, and Madam Wu. The master of ceremonies stopped them, pointing down the steps: commoners could not sit among ministers and nobles. Liu Yu unbuckled his sword and handed it to the gate guard.
“If there aren’t enough seats, we can move the meeting outside.”

Sima Dewen stood at the top of the stairs. He saw the muddy old straw sandals rolled in Madam Wu’s arms, hesitated, and let them enter. Ministers sat in front; the commoners were seated in the rear gallery. Madam Wu remained standing, afraid the mud on the sandals would soil the palace’s brocade cushions.

Three grain registers lay on the table: one from the old Jingkou troops, one from Jiankang’s navy, and one covering what the city wards had supplied. Liu Yu placed them side by side and had each camp’s grain officer verify his marks. Grain requisitioned on the same day from the same storehouse had been entered in two separate books, each as a first issue. The clerks checking the ledgers were drenched in sweat.

“Count only the fighting men and the grain will last four months,” Liu Yu said, pointing to the figures. “Include rations for the people, medicines for the wounded, and the boat crews quartered in the city, and we have less than two. We have a little over two hundred and seventy serviceable warships, fewer than a hundred capable of carrying heavily armored troops. Thirty percent of our arrowheads remain. There are more than seventeen hundred wounded. Another died last night.”

Liu Yi wanted grain requisitioned from the great families' storehouses. An official under Wang Mi said several clans had already donated twice and still had thousands of tenants to feed on their estates. Liu Yi laughed coldly and asked whether they preferred to feed the living or keep full granaries for Qin to take. As they argued, the apothecary owner heard someone claim the city could hold out through winter. Unable to bear it, he left his seat and knelt.

“Grain can be borrowed. Medicine cannot. We have three days' supply of angelica root. For clean dressings we’ve been reduced to washing old mourning clothes. There are medicine merchants outside the walls, but the checkpoints stop them. Wait another winter, and all seventeen hundred wounded men will be lying outside the Eastern Headquarters.”

A censor said Qin traders might conceal spies and every package of medicine had to be inspected and sealed. The shopkeeper raised his head. “Then send someone to help me inspect them. My two assistants haven’t slept in three days. They know their medicines. They don’t know who is planning rebellion.”
Madam Wu suddenly said, “My boy has finished waiting.”

Liu Yu passed the medicine shortages to the officer responsible for closing the gates. As the man took the document, a piece of sealing wax from a warehouse showed at his sleeve. It emerged that another military order had caused three boats of hemp cloth to be impounded the night before. Someone in the hall muttered a curse. Outside, a young palace attendant hurried up with news that soldiers requisitioning grain in Yongxing Ward had come to blows with residents.

Ward Head Ge took yesterday’s grain receipt from his robe. It had been folded in quarters; sweat had soaked the red seal. They had surrendered forty-three shi of grain the night before. Now the navy had come, insisting yesterday’s levy belonged to the Eastern Headquarters and did not count toward naval provisions. Gripping the corner of the receipt, Ge held it up to the ministers. “How many times do the generals mean to eat, that one ward must pay for every meal?”

Liu Yi turned pale at the genuine seal. He had ordered only ten days' additional rations for each camp; his subordinates had levied them separately, camp by camp. Liu Yu did not take the opportunity to humiliate him. He ordered a Secretariat clerk to seal both sets of military orders, and halted all grain levies not verified against the central army’s master register, lest the city break into fighting before the debate was over.
That suspension made the hall noisier still.

Sima Dewen insisted that the Jin ancestral temples must be preserved. He invoked the century since the court and its nobles crossed south, saying no imperial kinsman had the right to sign an edict extinguishing the dynasty on behalf of the departed emperors. Liu Yi would no longer stake the lives of tens of thousands in the Beifu Army upon some unknown future edict from the Sima house. He said plainly that Jiangnan needed a ruler who could command its armies and govern its commanderies and counties.

He Wuji struck the table and sprang up, accusing him of plotting an internal struggle with Qin troops at the gates. The great families around them were scarcely of one mind. Those whose estates lay in the Three Wu districts wished to preserve their property; those whose homes stood near the outer walls feared another two months would leave them ashes. Some hoped Qin would stop north of the Yangtze, yet secretly sent servants to the Qin camp to inquire about its new land-registration laws.

Two Beifu veterans began quarreling as well. One man’s father had died fighting northern cavalry and would never have bowed to them. The other’s younger brother had survived because of a medical camp in Qin territory; he knew that statutes written in Guanzhong could put a value on a human life, too. Each called the other heartless, and they nearly overturned the water cups on their mats. Liu Yu did not silence them. When he met Fu Jian at the Fei River, he could still declare that the people of Jiangnan would not let others hand them over. Watching the men argue until their faces burned red, he realized a single treaty might have to carry many demands that contradicted one another.
In the afternoon Liu Yi finally pointed straight at the empty throne.

“Jinu, the Sima house can no longer govern the people. You’ve earned your victories; you have soldiers and generals. Take the throne today, issue an edict to put the grain under one command, and the Beifu Army may yet fight on.”
Several officers looked toward the imperial steps. Even the master of ceremonies forgot to straighten the mats.

Liu Yu looked at the throne, so seldom occupied now. Years earlier in Jingkou he had begged for military households' land deeds and waited outside the mansions of powerful men to be admitted. When Huan Xuan’s new regime had suppressed claims for unpaid grain, he had asked himself why it was always someone else who got to sit there. He had no need to pretend the thought had never occurred to him.
“I have thought of it,” he said.
Liu Yi immediately took half a step forward.
“But if I sat there today, would there be any more grain in the warehouses?”
Liu Yi said a new dynasty could seize the great families' private stores by force, unite the generals' armies, and end the issuing of separate orders from every camp.
“And when we’ve seized it all?”

The granary officer hesitated before reporting that all the clans' stores together would last another four or five months. After that they would have to seize the river supply routes and conscript more able-bodied men from the city. At the words “conscript more men,” Madam Wu gripped a crack in the old paint on the pillar.

Liu Yu climbed the stone steps. His palm came to rest upon the arm of the throne, then drew away. He had governed three counties from Jingkou, corrected military households' land registers, and punished soldiers for stealing grain. In Danyang, where the fields were somewhat more extensive, a single old deed could give rise to seven or eight competing claims. If he took the throne now, every person who asked why he was requisitioning grain again would first have to bear the accusation of disloyalty to a new dynasty.
“I can fight my way into this city,” he said to Liu Yi. “I’ve done it before. Keeping it alive now may take more than a sword. A ledger may serve us better.”
“Are you going to call yourself a subject?” Liu Yi asked coldly.
“First we negotiate. If Qin leaves our people no way to live, we go on fighting.”
“You know what those negotiations will end in.”
“I know.”

He said nothing more. Liu Yi sat down in anger, and for a time nobody could offer another way forward. The rain had stopped outside the hall, but drops still fell from the gallery tiles into a full earthen basin in the courtyard, each making a small, distinct sound.

The first dispute over the draft treaty concerned the ancestral temples. Sima Dewen refused to let the temple keepers open them for a new dynasty. Others of the imperial clan feared that if they defended the city for another two months there might not even be rice left for sacrifices. Ward Head Ge pulled a creased tenant’s contract from his sleeve and asked the ministers whether a truce meant anything if, afterward, a former landlord could use such a paper to carry away the people who cultivated his fields. Only after another argument did they write into the draft that the temples must not be destroyed, claims to land must be verified one by one, and no person could be detained as private property.

The apothecary owner wanted medicine boats admitted at three ferries. A military officer, fearing crossbow mechanisms hidden in medicine chests, told him to open each chest for inspection. Instead the shopkeeper set his herb list beside the imperial desk, pointed to the words “Life-Restoring Powder,” and asked who would collect the bodies from the Eastern Headquarters if inspection took another half day. Yuan Liu the boatman named the three vessels of cloth detained the previous week and could even say which oar had cracked. Zhu Xu asked that inspection of each boat and a right of appeal against mistaken detention be written into the same clause. The Beifu generals then argued over back pay and compensation for the dead, until the hall rang with names demanding verification.
“File them and put them under seal,” Liu Yu said.
“The very name of the Beifu Army, too?”
“The living still need their pay.”

He Wuji pressed a hand to his knee and asked no more for a long while. Under Xie Xuan he had seen that banner rise in the river wind. He knew a flag could not buy even a handful of grain; he also knew some men had crawled back from among the dead because they had seen it flying. Liu Yu did not demand his assent that day. He allowed Wuji’s dissent to be attached to the minutes.

The hardest matter was whether Liu Yu would stay or go. Wang Mi did not want military power throughout Jiangnan entrusted to one man; the old Beifu generals wanted even less to see him taken north to Chang’an as a captive. Standing in the rear gallery, Madam Wu suddenly asked, “If you’re afraid of his soldiers, couldn’t the court take some of them and leave him here to check the accounts?”

The ministers turned to her. The old woman knew she had put it crudely, but held her ground. Liu Muzhi quietly observed that a provisional regional administration with periodic reviews was possible. Liu Yu could oversee Jiangnan’s military and civil affairs for the time being, while troop transfers and appointments required a second signature and remained open to formal objection. At last the ministers had something on paper worth arguing over.

By afternoon the draft had twenty-one articles. For every addition or deletion, someone wrote down, on the spot, why he opposed it. Liu Yu forbade the ceremonial officers to copy these objections as “the unanimous assent of the ministers.” If tomorrow they expected people to obey a difficult provision, they ought at least to know who had accepted it today, and at what cost.

Toward evening the Qin army returned two hundred and thirty-seven wounded soldiers ahead of any agreement. Their escorts accepted only the previously agreed certificates of injury; nobody demanded a handprint pledging surrender. As the wounded passed through Vermilion Bird Gate, townspeople crowded the streets looking for familiar faces. One soldier with a severed leg was being carried by a comrade. Madam Wu pushed through the throng and caught his worn sleeve.
“Eastern Headquarters, Fifth Camp. Did you know Wu A-Si?”
He had. The boy had cried out in pain until his voice grew faint. The soldier did not invent a final cry of “Mother” for Madam Wu, nor tell her that A-Si had died without bitterness.
The old woman stood there a long time. Only after the column had passed did she ask Liu Yu, “Did you correct the surname?”
“I did.” He had the military-register officer open the roll before her. Madam Wu touched the character, checked that its strokes were finally right, and turned away.
“Did you settle anything today?”
“We have a draft. Zhu Xu will take it to the northern camp. Then we wait for their answer.”
“Make it quick.”
Holding the straw sandals, she walked home along the street. Liu Yu watched her pass a row of shopfronts whose boards had only just been removed, then ordered the lamps lit.

That night Zhu Xu left the city with the draft agreed upon in Jiankang. The seal case held not only the council’s signatures, but a casualty roll still incomplete and unverified. A gate soldier held his horse and asked whether the Qin ruler would accept all twenty-one articles. Zhu Xu touched the brass clasp of the case. “Both sides will strike out a few lines. I only hope that when they do, they’ll remember the names of living people written on those pages.”
The gates closed again. Zhu Xu rode toward the Qin camp. Behind him the palace bells had fallen silent, but wounded men at the Eastern Headquarters were still crying out in the night.
